questions.q: In this lesson's terms, what is a stakeholder's first complaint usually considered?
options: A fully specified requirement ready to design against
A symptom, not yet a requirement
An irrelevant detail that should be ignored
A technical specification
questions.explain: The lesson uses 'people are confused about approval' as an example symptom that discovery turns into a specific root cause.

questions.q: Why does the discovery question "who should be involved" need to produce a named role, not just "someone in management"?
options: Because Salesforce requires a specific username in every approval process
Management always refuses to be named
A vague answer can't be translated into a concrete approver assignment the way a named role can
It doesn't matter -- any answer works the same way
questions.explain: Designs like Lesson 11's approval process need a specific approver (owner's manager, Sales Director) -- a vague answer can't be configured.

questions.q: Why does the lesson include "how will we know this is fixed" among the discovery questions?
options: It forces a measurable outcome instead of a vague sense that things feel better
It is only relevant for approval processes, not other automation
It replaces the need for testing from Lesson 15
It is the least important of the discovery questions
questions.explain: A measurable outcome, like zero scheduling conflicts, gives the design something concrete to be checked against later.

questions.q: According to the lesson, where did the specific numbers in Lesson 14's Mill Creek brief (over 5 days, 2 conflicts) most plausibly come from?
options: A random number generator
Salesforce's default approval process settings
Guesswork by the automation builder
A real discovery conversation asking exactly what triggers the problem
questions.explain: HR would not necessarily volunteer those specifics unprompted -- a well-asked discovery question is what produces that precision.

questions.q: What risk does designing automation straight from a symptom, without discovery, create?
options: The automation will always run slower
The design might fix the wrong thing, such as adding a reminder instead of building actual entry criteria
Salesforce will reject the automation at save time
There is no risk -- symptoms and root causes are interchangeable
questions.explain: The lesson's example shows a symptom-level fix (a confusion reminder) missing the actual root cause (no entry criteria at all).
